In brief

When Stephen has finished describing Shakespeare's wife as a beautiful seductress, his listeners (Eglinton, Best, Russell) crowd in with unrelated talk, and over the course of another paragraph Stephen silently reflects on their otherworldly preoccupations. His thoughts touch on a minor Dublin writer named "Louis H. Victory," and after contemplating quasi-Hindu mysteries he imperfectly recalls two lines of a poem by that man: "In quintessential triviality / For years in this fleshcase a shesoul dwelt." The quotation is of a piece with Theosophical spiritualism, but its striking word "shesoul" also glances back at Anne Hathaway, insinuating a contrast between her sexual immoderation and the men's asexual idealism.

At more length

Victory is probably on Stephen's radar because eight years earlier he had published a book titled The Higher Teaching of Shakespeare. The book was dedicated "To George W. Russell ('Æ'), Friend, Poet, and Mystic," and its study of the Bard's "profound 'soul-wisdom'" (viii) is exactly the kind of Shakespeare criticism that Stephen is determined to combat in his talk. The book studies fourteen plays. In Macbeth, "conscience is unveiled and shown forth as a working spiritual essence" (1). In King Lear everlasting Truth is a "gem that shimmers before our soul-eyes" (16), showing Shakespeare to be "a master of the whole metaphysics of humanity" (17). The Merchant of Venice demonstrates the dangers of grounding one's hopes on Chance. Romeo and Juliet exemplifies the moral that "Out of Evil cometh Good." And so forth. These Higher Teachings smooth out all the critical wrinkles, enigmas, contradictions, and complexities in the plays, making them occasions for edifying moral reflection.

As far as I can tell Stephen does not engage with any of Victory's critical observations in his own remarks on particular plays. He thinks only of some lines from "Soul-Perturbating Mimicry," a poem that Victory published in Poems (1895) and again in Imaginations in the Dust (1903). In the manner of John Donne's The First Anniversary and The Second Anniversary (1611-12), this lyric finds spiritual truths revealed in the death of an angelic young girl. The first of four stanzas reads:

In quintessential triviality
Of flesh, for four fleet years, a she-soul dwelt.
Oft, unpremeditatedly, I knelt
In meads, where round this thought-refining she,
To sun me in the God-light mystery,
That I, love-chained and beauty pinioned, felt
Flashed from her, hieroglyphically spelt,
Like gifts that fall from white Austerity.

Joyce evidently relied on memory to quote from these lines, since "for four fleet years" has become "For years" and the trivial flesh a soul-harboring "fleshcase." But the key word for his purposes is the peculiar "shesoul." Stephen recalls it because he has been speaking of Anne Hathaway and then thinking of soul-worshipers. In his mind the two are antithetical. Later in Scylla and Charybdis, focusing again on Anne, he scathingly remarks that "In old age she takes up with gospellers (one stayed at New Place and drank a quart of sack the town paid for but in which bed he slept it skills not to ask) and heard she had a soul." In his imagination Anne is a libidinous creature, interested only in matters of the flesh. Nothing could be further from Victory's ethereal "thought-refining she."

Between the mention of Victory's name and the quotation of his verses, Stephen employs the strange word as he thinks of Theosophists contemplating their astral realities: "Lotus ladies tend them i'the eyes, their pineal glands aglow. Filled with his god, he thrones, Buddh under plantain. Gulfer of souls, engulfer. Hesouls, shesouls, shoals of souls." Mockery bleeds through in his echo of a childish tongue-twister, "She sells seashells down by the seashore."

Other childish word games have been dancing through Stephen's head. When John Eglinton says that "Piper is coming" to Moore's soirée, the narrator mockingly mimes the name ("— Piper! Mr Best piped. Is Piper back?"), and then Stephen makes hash of it with a tongue-twister: "Peter Piper pecked a peck of pick of peck of pickled pepper." When he imagines spiritual questers circling about a holy figure, possibly George Russell ("The faithful hermetists await the light, ripe for chelaship, ringroundabout him"), he is probably thinking of the nursery rhyme, "Ring around a rosy, / A pocket full of posies, / Ashes, ashes, / We all fall down."

All this prattle works to undermine Victory's conceit of a little girl in whom "the God-light mystery" shines. It is as if Stephen is thinking, "This is how four-year-olds really talk." But something more than mere mockery seems to be going on in the sentences immediately before and after the tongue-twister: "Gulfer of souls, engulfer. Hesouls, shesouls, shoals of souls. Engulfed with wailing creecries, whirled, whirling, they bewail." These words paint a more haunting picture of the mystically rapt or postmortemic soul-states that the Theosophists spend their days contemplating.

Gifford glosses "Gulfer of souls" as "God, who in Theosophical terms cast souls out of himself into himself, since all souls are one with God and came from him. The vast majority of souls in earthly life forget their God-source though still contained within him." Slote, Mamigonian, and Turner look instead to the Odyssey. Noting that the OED defines the verb "gulf" as "to swallow up in a whirlpool," they quote from Homer's description of Charybdis as a monster that "sucks down the black water." Different as these readings are, they may both be correct. In Scylla and Charybdis the whirlpool stands symbolically for spiritual idealism and disembodiment. The engulfing of souls in mystical oneness is an attractive force that the artist must avoid. Shakespeare and Stephen, like Odysseus, need to "Hold to the here, the now, through which all future plunges to the past."

As for those "wailing creecries" and their "whirling," they too sound metaphysical notes derived from epic literature. Canto 5 of Dante's Inferno is the likeliest source. In the first circle of Hell, those who have been damned for their lustful actions appear as a swarm of birdlike souls driven back and forth by violent winds. Dante hears "a great wailing" (27) as the sinners "shriek, weep, and lament" (35), and he sees a squall that "whirls and strikes" them (33). (The Hollanders' translation, used everywhere on this website, serendipitously reproduces Joyce's words.)

Alternatively, it is possible that Joyce is continuing to recall passages from the Odyssey. In a personal communication, Vincent Van Wyk suggests the relevance of the opening lines of book 24, where Hermes leads the spirits of the slaughtered suitors out of the palace. There the spirits "squeak" (9) like terrified little animals, "squeaking / like bats in secret crannies of a cave" (5-6). The passage mentions no whirling, but bats do whirl, and in this passage Hermes is an engulfer of souls. Whether Stephen is thinking of tortured adulterers or slaughtered suitors, in either case the associations are not good.

John Hunt 2026
